prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current safety mechanisms for Large Language Models (LLMs)—such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and perplexity filtering—are trained primarily on natural language or common, static encodings (e.g., Base64, ROT13). Existing "jailbreak" methods largely rely on fixed prompt templates or white-box optimization techniques that require access to gradients or token probabilities. These approaches are often brittle; fixed encodings are easily patched, and white-box attacks do not transfer well to closed API-based models. There is currently a lack of **dynamic, black-box attack methodologies** that can systematically bypass safety filters by exploiting the model's own capabilities to learn and reason in real-time, without relying on pre-existing knowledge of specific ciphers.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the advanced **In-Context Learning (ICL)** capabilities of frontier models can be weaponized against them. We hypothesize that if we "teach" an LLM a novel, randomly generated mapping (a bijection) within the prompt itself, the model will be able to interpret and process queries in this obfuscated format.

Our intuition is twofold:
1.  **Safety Bypass:** The safety guardrails (often shallower or separate classifiers) will fail to recognize the intent behind the obfuscated query because the encoding is generated randomly on the fly and does not match any training distribution.
2.  **Scale-Adaptivity:** Unlike traditional attacks that become harder as models get safer, this attack should become *more* effective as models become more capable. We hypothesize that stronger models with superior reasoning skills will be better at learning complex bijections in-context, thereby successfully executing instructions that weaker models (or safety filters) cannot parse.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We aim to develop a framework for **Bijection Learning**, effectively acting as a "prompt fuzzer" that generates infinite variations of encoding attacks. The workflow is designed as follows:

1.  **Procedural Mapping Generation:**
    We will develop a module to generate random, bijective (one-to-one) string-to-string mappings. Instead of using standard ciphers, we will create custom "languages" where English characters map to arbitrary tokens (e.g., permuted letters, multi-digit numbers, or symbols). We will introduce **complexity parameters** (such as "dispersion" or "encoding length") to tune the difficulty of the mapping, allowing us to match the encoding complexity to the target model's capability.

2.  **In-Context Teaching Pipeline:**
    We will construct prompts that utilize few-shot learning to teach the target model this new mapping dynamically. The prompt structure will include:
    *   **System Instructions:** Explicit rules defining the transformation logic.
    *   **Translation Examples:** Pairs of benign text in English and the generated bijection language to demonstrate the pattern.
    *   **Encoded Payload:** The harmful query, translated into the bijection language, positioned as the final user turn.

3.  **decoding and Denoising:**
    Upon receiving the model's response (which we expect to be in the bijection language), we will deterministically map it back to English using the inverse of our generated function. To handle potential imperfections in the model's output (e.g., typos in the cipher), we will employ a lightweight "denoising" step (potentially using a smaller helper model) to reconstruct the plain text for verification.

4.  **Best-of-N Sampling:**
    Since the space of possible bijections is combinatorially large, we will implement a sampling strategy. For any single harmful intent, we will generate multiple distinct bijections. This turns the attack into a probabilistic search, where we only need *one* mapping to successfully bypass the filter while remaining intelligible to the model.

## Expected Contribution
We anticipate this work will establish a new class of **universal, black-box jailbreaks** that exploit the fundamental feature of modern LLMs: their ability to learn from context. Theoretically, this will demonstrate a "Pareto frontier" of vulnerability, providing evidence that increased model capability (specifically in reasoning and instruction following) can directly correlate with increased safety risks. This will shift the red-teaming paradigm from finding static "magic words" to generating dynamic, complexity-controlled adversarial languages.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated the efficacy of "bijection learning" attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs). This method leverages in-context learning to teach a model a bijective mapping (encoding) and subsequently submits a harmful query encoded in that mapping.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **AdvBench-50:** A subset of harmful intents (Chao et al., 2023).
    *   **HarmBench:** The full test set comprising 320 harmful behaviors/intents.
    *   **HarmBench-35:** A sampled subset of 35 intents from HarmBench (5 intents from each risk category).
    *   **Benign Dataset:** A custom dataset of 100 unambiguously benign intents used for evaluating false positive rates in guarded systems.
    *   **MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding):** Used to measure capability degradation under bijection encodings (10-shot setup).

*   **Models Evaluated:**
    *   **Target Models:** Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o.
    *   **Llama 3.1 & Gemini 1.5:** Referenced in scaling law analysis (Llama 3.1 8B It, Llama 3.1 70B It, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro).
    *   **Guard Models:** Llama Guard-style prompted classifiers using GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3 Haiku, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet as the backend.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Attack Success Rate (ASR):** The percentage of intents for which the attack elicits a response classified as "unsafe."
    *   **Judgment Protocol:** A hybrid approach. First, GPT-4o-mini classifies harmfulness using the HarmBench classifier prompt. Second, human evaluators filter the "unsafe" results to remove false positives.
    *   **"PREFS" Criteria:** Human judges confirmed a response was unsafe only if it was Practical, Relevant, Egregious, Factually correct, and Specific.
    *   **Failure Mode Classification:** Responses categorized as "Canned refusal" (detected via string matching), "Incoherency" (jumbled text/repetition), or "Unhelpfulness" (generic follow-ups), determined by a GPT-4o-mini classifier.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **GCG Transfer:** Greedy Coordinate Gradient (white-box suffix optimization) trained on Llama Guard 3 and transferred to target.
    *   **PAIR:** Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement (black-box, attacker model refines prompt).
    *   **TAP:** Tree of Attacks with Pruning (black-box, tree-search). Attack budget set to 58 (branching 3, width 5, depth 5).
    *   **Encoding Ensemble:** A collection of 11 encoding-based attacks (ASCII, Base64, leetspeak, ROT13, Morse code, Caesar cipher, Self-Cipher, keyboard cipher, upside-down cipher, word reversal, grid cipher). Success defined as at least 1 of 11 succeeding.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Bijection Learning Method:** System prompt explains the mapping; Multi-turn history provides "teaching examples" (Paul Graham essays) and "practice examples" (conversation with Claude 3.5 Sonnet); Final user message contains the encoded harmful query.
    *   **Complexity Parameters:**
        *   **Codomain:** Target of the mapping (e.g., letters, $\ell$-digit numbers, tokens).
        *   **Dispersion ($d$):** Number of letters mapping to non-self values.
        *   **Encoding Length ($\ell$):** Number of characters in the mapped output.
    *   **Inference:** Temperature 0.
    *   **Sampling:** Best-of-$n$ sampling (Attack Budget).
    *   **Post-processing:** Responses decoded via inverse mapping and denoised using GPT-4o-mini to correct minor spelling errors.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Attack Efficacy and Scaling:**
*   **Observation:** Bijection learning achieved an ASR of 86.3% against Claude 3.5 Sonnet on HarmBench, outperforming the ensemble of 11 previous encoding attacks by over 60 percentage points (Ensemble ASR was 20.9%).
*   **Observation:** Increasing the attack budget (Best-of-$n$) significantly improved ASR. For Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ASR improved from ~46.2% at budget $n=1$ to 86.2% at budget $n=24$.
*   **Observation:** GPT-4o-mini showed an increase from 13.8% ($n=1$) to 58.1% ($n=20$).

**Impact of Dispersion and Bijection Type (Ablation Data):**
*   **Observation:** We measured ASR on HarmBench-35 with attack budget $n=6$ across different dispersion levels.
    *   **Claude 3 Haiku (Digit Bijection):** ASR was 46% ($d=3$), 60% ($d=6$), 71% ($d=8$), 26% ($d=11$), and 0% ($d=16$).
    *   **Claude 3 Haiku (Letter Bijection):** ASR was 40% ($d=3$), 60% ($d=6$), 69% ($d=8$), 74% ($d=11$), and 54% ($d=16$).
    *   **GPT-4o-mini (Digit Bijection):** ASR was 26% ($d=3$), 31% ($d=6$), 9% ($d=8$), and 0% ($d=11$).
    *   **GPT-4o-mini (Letter Bijection):** ASR was 26% ($d=3$), 29% ($d=6$), 43% ($d=8$), 26% ($d=11$), and 0% ($d=16$).
*   **Observation:** A "middling" range of dispersion yielded the strongest attacks. Very high dispersion caused models to fail to learn the mapping (ASR dropped to 0%), while very low dispersion failed to bypass safety filters.
*   **Observation:** Letter-to-digit bijections were observed to be more difficult for models to learn than letter-to-letter bijections.

**Failure Mode Analysis:**
*   **Observation:** We identified three primary failure modes: Canned refusal, Incoherency, and Unhelpfulness.
*   **Observation:** For Claude 3 Haiku (2-digit bijection), as dispersion increased from 2 to 16:
    *   **Refusal Rate:** Decreased from ~5% to 0%.
    *   **Incoherency/Unhelpfulness:** Increased from ~5% ($d=2$) to ~65% ($d=16$).
    *   **Jailbreak Success:** Peaked at $d=8$ (~25%) and dropped to ~3% at $d=16$.
*   **Observation:** For GPT-4o-mini (2-digit bijection), refusal rates started high (~65% at $d=2$) and dropped to <5% at $d=16$. Incoherency rose sharply, reaching >85% at $d=16$.

**Capabilities Degradation (MMLU):**
*   **Observation:** MMLU accuracy (10-shot) decreased monotonically as bijection dispersion and encoding length increased.
*   **Observation:** Claude 3.5 Sonnet maintained >90% MMLU accuracy for letter bijections but dropped to <40% for 4-digit bijections at high dispersion.
*   **Observation:** GPT-4o-mini showed a steeper decline, dropping from ~80% accuracy (dispersion 3, letter) to ~30% (dispersion 16, letter).

**Scaling Laws and Pareto Frontiers:**
*   **Observation:** We observed a Pareto frontier between model capabilities (MMLU score) and Jailbreak Efficacy (HarmBench-35 ASR).
*   **Observation:** Attack efficacy peaked in the transition between a "scaling regime" (where unsafe responses became more coherent) and a "saturated regime" (where capabilities were high enough to trigger refusals).
*   **Observation:** More capable models (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet vs. Haiku) exhibited peak attack effectiveness at higher levels of bijection complexity.

**Defense with Guarded Systems:**
*   **Observation:** We tested a guarded system (Input/Output filtering) protecting a Claude 3.5 Sonnet target.
    *   **Unguarded Baseline:** 73.8% ASR.
    *   **GPT-4o-mini Guard:** Reduced ASR to 64.7%, but flagged 12.0% of benign intents.
    *   **Claude 3 Haiku Guard:** Reduced ASR to near-zero, but suffered from massive over-refusal, flagging 96.0% of benign intents.
    *   **Claude 3.5 Sonnet Guard:** Reduced ASR to 63.7%, with 0% false positives on benign intents.
*   **Observation:** Even a guard model with capability parity (Sonnet guarding Sonnet) only reduced ASR by approximately 10 percentage points (73.8% to 63.7%).

**Risk Categories:**
*   **Observation:** On Claude 3.5 Sonnet, the attack was most effective in "Illegal," "Cybercrime," and "Chemical/Biological" risk categories, with ASRs exceeding 80% in these sectors.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures

\begin{center}

```

\label{sample-table}

\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\

Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current safety mechanisms for Large Language Models (LLMs)—including RLHF, perplexity filtering, and input/output guardrails—rely heavily on detecting harmful intent within interpretable text or recognized patterns. While optimization-based attacks exist, they often require white-box access (gradients/logits) or produce unintelligible prompts that are easily filtered. Conversely, existing encoding-based attacks rely on the model’s *intrinsic* knowledge of fixed ciphers (e.g., Base64, ROT13), which are finite and easily patched.

A significant gap exists in the domain of black-box, universal jailbreaks. Specifically, there is no framework that exploits the **in-context learning (ICL)** capabilities of frontier models to dynamically generate and utilize *new*, arbitrary communication protocols. We posit that as models scale, their ability to learn complex rules on-the-fly increases, potentially rendering them more vulnerable to obfuscation attacks that weaker models cannot comprehend. We lack a method to procedurally generate these obfuscations to conduct "prompt fuzzing" without relying on static, pre-trained cipher knowledge.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **Bijection Learning**, a novel attack algorithm that leverages in-context learning to teach LLMs arbitrary, randomized bijective mappings (string-to-string encodings) immediately prior to delivering a harmful payload.

Our core hypothesis is that by forcing the model to operate within a newly learned, complex linguistic transformation layer, we can bypass safety training that generalizes poorly to out-of-distribution (obfuscated) inputs. Furthermore, we hypothesize a **scale-adaptive vulnerability**: stronger models with superior in-context learning capabilities will be more susceptible to high-complexity bijection attacks than weaker models, as the latter will fail to learn the mapping and simply produce incoherent outputs. By parametrizing the complexity of these bijections, we can control the trade-off between the model's ability to follow instructions and its ability to detect safety violations.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will design a black-box attack framework that generates random bijective encodings, instructs the target model to learn them via few-shot prompting, and manages the translation of inputs and outputs.

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of Bijections
We define the source alphabet $\Sigma$ as the standard English alphabet. We will generate a bijective function $f: \Sigma \rightarrow C$, where $C$ is a target codomain of strings.

We will implement three specific types of codomains for $C$:
1.  **Permuted Alphabet:** $C = \Sigma$, where letters map to other letters.
2.  **Numeric Sequences:** $C \subset \{0, \dots, 9\}^\ell$, where letters map to unique $\ell$-digit numbers.
3.  **Tokenizer Tokens:** $C$ consists of distinct tokens from the target model's vocabulary.

To modulate the difficulty of the attack, we will define and control two complexity parameters:
*   **Encoding Length ($\ell$):** The number of characters in the target string for each mapping (e.g., mapping 'a' to '1' vs '01' vs '001').
*   **Dispersion ($d$):** The number of source characters that do *not* map to themselves. Formally:
    $$d = |\{x \in \Sigma \mid f(x) \neq x\}|$$
    A dispersion of $d=0$ represents plaintext; $d=26$ represents a full substitution cipher.

### 2. Attack Protocol and Prompt Architecture
The attack will proceed in a "prompt fuzzing" manner via **Best-of-$n$ sampling**. For a given harmful intent $x$, we will sample $n$ random bijections $\{f_1, \dots, f_n\}$ and attempt to jailbreak the model with each.

The prompt structure for each attempt will consist of three distinct segments tailored to induce in-context learning:

1.  **System Instruction:** A step-by-step definition of the randomly generated bijection $f$.
    *   *Draft Content:* "You are about to learn a new language... The characters in the English alphabet map to... {dictionary of mappings}."
2.  **Teaching Examples (Multi-turn ICL):** We will provide $k_t$ turns of examples.
    *   **User Message:** Benign text $T_{eng}$ (e.g., essays or general knowledge).
    *   **Assistant Message:** The translation $T_{enc} = f(T_{eng})$ in the bijection language.
3.  **Practice Examples:** $k_p$ turns of conversational history where the User and Assistant converse entirely in the encoded language to stabilize the model's adherence to the mapping.
4.  **Attack Payload:** The final User message will be the encoded harmful intent: $x_{enc} = f(x)$.

### 3. Response Decoding and Denoising
Upon receiving the model's response $r_{enc}$ (which we expect to be in the bijection language), we will apply the inverse mapping $f^{-1}$ to recover the plaintext response $r_{raw}$.

We anticipate that models may introduce stochastic errors (spelling mistakes or extra tokens) when generating output in a newly learned language. To address this, we will implement a **Denoising Module**.
*   We will prompt an auxiliary model (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to correct minor decoding errors in $r_{raw}$ to produce the final clean response $r_{final}$.
*   The denoiser will be strictly instructed to correct spelling/formatting without adding new content.

### 4. Implementation Details
*   **Sampling Strategy:** We will utilize temperature sampling on the generation of the bijections themselves, effectively creating an endless pool of unique attack prompts for a single intent.
*   **Validation:** We will define success if at least one of the $n$ prompts results in a harmful response that is coherent and relevant after decoding.

## Expected Contribution
This project aims to establish **Bijection Learning** as a primary mechanism for understanding the intersection of capability and safety.
1.  **Universal Black-Box Attack:** We expect to provide a method that works on any instruction-following model without access to gradients or tokenizers.
2.  **Scale-Adaptivity:** We intend to demonstrate that this attack vector becomes *more* potent as models scale, providing empirical evidence that advanced reasoning capabilities (specifically in-context learning) can be weaponized to bypass safety training.
3.  **Procedural Fuzzing:** By quantifying encoding complexity (dispersion and length), we will provide a framework for "infinite" prompt generation, moving beyond static libraries of hand-crafted jailbreaks.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
